title: How much is it? — shopping and bargaining
goal: Ask prices, read Vietnamese money with all its zeros, and bargain politely — including spotting a small trap called *rưỡi*.
bekal: ask for and understand prices in hundreds of thousands of *đồng*
name colors and sizes, and ask to try things with *thử*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ở chợ Đồng Xuân
dialogs.intro: Đồng Xuân Market, Hà Nội. Budi is looking for shirts to take home as gifts. At markets like this prices aren't marked, and bargaining isn't just allowed — it's expected.

notes: ⚠️ **Rưỡi means "and a half of the unit just mentioned"**, and with money it comes up all the time: *hai trăm rưỡi* = 250,000 (two hundred **thousand** and a half), *bốn trăm rưỡi* = 450,000. Not 200.5 and not 400.5. It's the same word as in *hai giờ rưỡi* in Unit 8 — and needs the same attention.

**Đồng is almost always dropped, and nghìn often is too.** The vendor says *ba trăm* and means *ba trăm nghìn đồng* — 300,000. Since prices under a thousand đồng practically don't exist anymore, nobody gets confused. For a foreigner that's scary on day one, so remember: **if the number sounds small, add "thousand" in your head**.

**Bớt means "reduce", and it's the bargaining verb.** The full polite sentence: *Chị bớt cho em một chút được không?* Shorter: *Bớt chút đi chị.* Note the *cho em* inside — "for me" — which makes the request sound like asking a favor, not making a demand.

**Notice that the pronouns have changed from earlier dialogues.** Budi calls the vendor *chị* and refers to himself as *em*, not *tôi*. At the market, family words like these make bargaining feel warm and almost always get you a better price. *Tôi* isn't wrong, but it sounds distant.

**Thử means "try" and goes AFTER the verb**: *mặc thử* (try on — literally "wear try"), *ăn thử* (try eating, taste), *đi thử* (try walking). English puts "try" first; Vietnamese puts the action first and the trying after. Practice it until it feels natural.
**Thôi được means "oh, all right then"** — the sign that bargaining is over and a deal has been struck. When you hear it, stop haggling; pushing further after *thôi được* is considered bad form.

grammars.title: Vietnamese money: reading numbers full of zeros
body: The currency is the *đồng*, and the smallest note still in use is 1,000. That's why almost every everyday price is counted in **nghìn** (thousands).

head: Amount
Tiếng Việt
Short form people actually say
Roughly
rows: an iced tea and a snack

after: ⚠️ ***Rưỡi* always means half of the unit right before it.** *Trăm rưỡi* = one hundred fifty thousand; *triệu rưỡi* = one and a half million. If in doubt, ask the vendor to write it down — *Chị viết ra được không?* — nobody finds that odd.
*Củ* is slang for "million", often heard at markets and among young people: *ba củ* = three million. You don't need to use it, but recognizing it can save you from an expensive misunderstanding.

grammars.title: Bargaining in five sentences
body: The order is almost always the same, and a whole bargaining session can be done with these five sentences.

head: Step
Tiếng Việt
Meaning
rows: *Chị bớt cho em một chút được không?*
Could you take a little off?
OK, I'll take it. / Maybe next time.

after: ⚠️ **The second option in step five is the real weapon.** *Thôi, để lần sau.* ("oh well, maybe next time"), said as you walk away, is the most effective and most polite way to bring the price down. If the vendor calls you back, the price really can drop; if not, the price was already fair.

**Bargaining is normal at traditional markets and souvenir shops, but NOT in supermarkets, cafés, or anywhere prices are marked.** Haggling where there's a price tag feels like haggling at a chain store — not offensive, just odd.

blocks.text: ⚠️ ***Màu xanh* means blue AND green at once.** To separate them, add a word: *xanh da trời* (sky blue) and *xanh lá cây* (leaf green). Vietnamese isn't the only language that merges the two, but for English speakers, who split blue and green from childhood, it's worth remembering when you order something.

Sizes use the English words as they are — *size S*, *size M*, *size L* — or the Vietnamese words *rộng* (too big), *chật* (too tight), *vừa* (just right). The sentences you need: *Có size to hơn không?* (do you have a bigger one?) and *Cái này chật quá.* (this is too tight).

head: Tiếng Việt
Say it
English
rows: Bớt cho em một chút đi.
Bớt cho em một chút di.

blocks.title: Two things that bring the price down by themselves
items: **Buying more than one.** *Em mua hai cái, chị bớt cho em nhé.* — this almost always works, and vendors are actually happy because their goods move faster.

**Speaking Vietnamese at all.** This isn't flattery: the price for a foreigner who bargains in Vietnamese is almost always different from the price for one who points and stays silent. The five sentences in the grammar box, said with tones accurate enough to be understood, are enough — a very concrete reason to practice your tones.
